title: Kernel selection safety envelope and ruin-recovery notes
content:
Purpose
- Capture an experimental framework for deciding when to prefer TensorRT kernels vs Triton-hosted kernels vs our custom CUDA ops.
- Define a "safety envelope" around numerical/functional correctness and latency tail risk, plus a "ruin-recovery" plan when a chosen path degrades in production.

Background / motivation
- We have three kernel modalities in flight: native TRT graph-compiled kernels (best throughput, sometimes numeric drift), Triton-backed reference kernels (stable numerics, higher baseline latency), and hand-rolled custom ops (good for specific attention patterns, moderate maintenance cost).
- Past incidents: small but customer-visible hallucination/regression after aggressive TRT-only rollout on long-context chat workloads (reported Dec 2024). We need an operational rulebook to avoid repeating that.

Definitions
- Safety envelope: a set of constraints (numeric tolerances, token-level divergence thresholds, output distribution checks, latency SLO limits) that a kernel selection must satisfy for a workload/model+config.
- Ruin-recovery: immediate and automated actions when production metrics indicate we are outside the safety envelope (e.g., switch routing, throttle batching, enable KV shadowing).
- Kernel hysteresis: conservative time/requests-based buffer to avoid flip-flopping between kernels during transient load/noise.

Heuristics proposed (selection stage)
1) Model profile + sequence length pre-checks:
   - If model uses fused custom attention patterns (e.g., rotary variants with specific ALiBi shaping), prefer custom kernels for seq_len >= 4096 unless quantization profile validated.
   - Otherwise, for medium seq (<=1024) prefer TRT in p95 throughput/cost-limited environments.
2) Quant-compatibility gate:
   - Maintain a per-model matrix of tested quant configs. If candidate (INT8/4-bit) profile has any failing regression tests (see test suite below), reject TRT-only route.
3) Numerics delta gate:
   - During canary, compute token-wise edit distance and log-prob KL between reference (Triton FP16 baseline) and candidate outputs on curated prompt set. Reject TRT selection if > 1.5% token divergence or KL > 0.25 on more than 2 prompts out of 200.
4) Latency tail gate:
   - If p99 latency of candidate kernel > deployed SLO * 1.2 for 5m sliding window, flag for local throttling.

Operational selection flow (runtime)
- Decision inputs: model_id, model_version, quant_profile, seq_len_histogram, recent_p95/p99 trends, canary_results, cached_kv_hit_rate.
- Score = alpha * expected_cost + beta * numeric_stability_score + gamma * p99_tail_risk. Tunable via feature flags.
- Precedence rules: safety gates (quant & numerics) are hard blocks; cost/latency are soft and trade-off via score.

KV cache considerations
- TRT path assumptions:
  - TRT kernels typically expect monolithic execution; fine-grained KV cache (prefix reuse) requires additional marshaling and may reduce throughput gains.
- Proposed modes:
  1) Full-KV-shadow mode: Always maintain reference KV service (Triton) shadow for verification during canary. Costly but safe for new model versions.
  2) Sparse-KV fallback: Keep a small cache of recent prefixes in Triton; route cold prefixes to TRT to benefit throughput but fall back on miss for correctness-sensitive routes (e.g., legal/reg-scrubbed content).

Ruin-recovery playbook (when envelope breached)
- Trigger conditions: sustained divergence alerts, content-pattern regressions, p99 SLO exceedance > 10% for 10 minutes, or safety test failures from integration harness.
- Immediate automated steps (order matters):
  1) Pause automatic routing to candidate kernel; route all traffic to Triton reference for affected model_version (fast rollback).
  2) Reduce batch sizes and disable batching heuristics that exacerbate tail latency.
  3) Enable KV-shadowing (route copies to both kernels and compare).
  4) Signal alerts with context snapshot (recent prompts, top n differing tokens, memory usage).
  5) Create a prioritized incident task with triage owner = model-onboarding lead.
- Human follow-up: review numerical diffs, run expanded evals, possibly retrain quant calibration tables.

Experiment plan (short-run)
- Objectives: quantify (1) numeric divergence between TRT FP16/INT8 vs Triton FP16, (2) p99 tail behavior across sequence lengths, (3) KV cache miss penalty when mixing kernels.
- Datasets: 1) curated canary prompts (200 prompts covering safety-sensitive patterns), 2) long-context synthetic streams (seq_len up to 8192), 3) production sample replay (anonymized, 1h window).
- Metrics:
  - numeric_divergence = fraction_of_tokens_where_top1_diff (per-prompt)
  - kl_divergence_topk = KL on top-k distributions
  - p95/p99 latency, throughput (tokens/sec), cost_per_token estimate
  - kv_miss_penalty_ms = extra latency on prefix miss when switching kernels
- Matrix of runs:
  - Baseline: Triton FP16
  - TRT FP16
  - TRT INT8 (calibrated)
  - Custom-op (where applicable)
  For each, run across seq buckets: 64, 512, 2048, 8192. Capture 30k tokens per run.

Preliminary findings (quick notes from initial lab runs)
- TRT FP16 gives 1.6x throughput on seq<=512 vs Triton; p99 improvement but at INT8 some prompts show token differences at first 20 tokens (~0.7% prompts).
- INT8 calibration is model-sensitive; calibration set must include long dynamic-range prompts or divergence spikes occur.
- KV miss penalty: 40-120ms extra when a prefix misses local TRT-placed cache and falls back to Triton; worst when miss rate > 15% for conversation workloads.
- Custom-op wins on long context attention kernels (seq>=4096) but has higher engineering maintenance; not safe to use without >500 run-hours of integration & CI coverage.

Test harness requirements (to operationalize gates)
- Auto-run of divergence tests on every model-version push: 200 canary prompts, report token divergence + KL. Must be in CI pipeline and produce machine-readable results stored in S3.
- Shadow run capability: route 1% of production traffic to candidate and store diffs for rolling analysis.
- Canary rollout automation: start at 0.1% traffic -> 1% -> 5% -> 20% with automated gates (numeric, latency). Each step requires pass or rollback.

Open questions / risks
- What is acceptable divergence threshold for generative models in product contexts? (need product input; legal/reg may need 0 tolerance for certain prompts.)
- Maintenance cost vs perf: custom ops reduce cost on niche long-context patterns but multiply CI & driver upgrade risk. How to amortize?
- Can we make KV cache format portable between kernels to avoid miss penalty? If we standardize KV serialization, does that hamper TRT optimization?

Action items
- (A1) Build CI job that runs token-divergence and top-k KL for each model+quant profile (owner: Rafael). Target: prototype by 2025-02-26.
- (A2) Implement lightweight shadowing toggle in routing layer (owner: Mei). Target: feature flag in two sprints.
- (A3) Run full experiment matrix on 3 representative models (chat-13b, instruct-7b, long-context-70b) and publish raw CSVs (owner: Aisha). Target: 2025-03-10.
- (A4) Proposal: define "safety envelope" JSON schema used by router config (draft by infra/product).

Notes to reviewers
- This document is intentionally pragmatic, not final. Looking for feedback on numeric gates, thresholds, and the practical operability of the ruin-recovery steps.
- Prefer conservative rollout defaults; performance wins can be pursued once safety gates are mature.

Appendix: example canary test output (mock)
- prompt_id: canary-042
  baseline_top1: "the user asked about billing"
  candidate_top1: "the user asked about billing"
  token_divergence: 0.0%
  kl_top10: 0.003
- prompt_id: canary-113
  baseline_top1: "the mitochondria is the powerhouse"
  candidate_top1: "mitochondria is the powerhouse"
  token_divergence: 2.1% 
  kl_top10: 0.45  <-- triggers reject

End.
